question: considering that the internet is a web of multiple systems, can there be a single event that completely brings it down?

inflammatory cells are generally overzealous and will do damage to things they shouldn't. it's a tradeoff, but a little extra damage or prolonged healing time is a small price to pay for staving off systemic bacterial infection. to further ensure that it doesn't get infected, his body sets up a pathway that makes him not want to touch that wound to anything; pain. 200,000 years later regular jack cuts his hand on the exact same stone (it could happen!). inflammatory cells rush into the wound and kick microbial ass. jack washes out the cut. he bandages it. it's clean now, and it's not open. if he touches the bandage to something, it doesn't really matter because the bandage makes an effective barrier between the wound and the outside world; the bacteria sit on the outside of the bandage until jack changes the dressing that evening. and then slathers it with diaf brand antibacterial ointment. the bacteria from the original wound were wiped out in the great peroxide flood of earlier this morning, and now any bacteria that may have hitched a ride nearby hits the gelatinous beast of pain and death as they drift near the wound. the bugs don't stand a chance against the concerted efforts of jack, an industrial society, and the local pharmacy. but those inflammatory cells are still operating under programming that is the result of hundreds of millions of years of evolution that each say "bacteria are freaking everywhere, and panic is the reasonable response here." so the inflammatory cells stay and play. but there is no tradeoff anymore. the risk of infection is greatly reduced, but the price of that constant patrol is the same as before. so regular jack takes 400mg of stfu brand ibuprofen which causes the inflammatory cells back off a bit, and the pain pathway eases up for a while. that is grossly oversimplified, but to give it a proper treatment would take a textbook or three.

question: is there any dark matter in my room right now?

question: why is it that during winter it's not uncommon to have days with abnormally high temperature and summer-like weather, but in the summer it never drops to winter-like weather for a day?
answer: hmm, lots of incomplete answers here. take a look at [this graph](_url_0_) of solar intensity vs latitude. as you can see, the summer pole receives about as much sunlight as the equator (actually, slightly more because of the 24-hour days in the arctic circle!). on the other hand, there's a huge difference in energy provided to the equator vs the completely dark winter pole. as a result, there's a huge difference in temperature between the winter pole and the equator, and not so much between the summer pole and equator. but that just explains changes in temperature vs *latitude*, not changes over time, so let's think about weather systems. storms are created by the north-south temperature gradient: as heat moves from equator to pole, a small amount of it is converted into kinetic energy. heat flow causes motion, just like a very inefficient steam or gasoline engine. when the temperature difference is large, the "engine" runs faster and more efficiently, creating more kinetic energy -- which is to say the storm winds blow stronger when the pole-equator temperature difference is large. so. in the wintertime, the difference in solar heating creates a much larger equator-pole temperature difference than in the summer. this creates much stronger wind patterns. so you've got stronger winds, blowing a bigger temperature gradient around across the surface of the earth ... so you see much bigger temperature shifts from day to day. edited to add some examples. here are views of temperatures and winds at the 500 mbar level [in northern hemisphere summer](_url_2_) (last august 19) and [northern hemisphere winter](_url_1_) (yesterday). colors indicate temperature contrast (purple is colder), streaks indicate wind direction and speed.

question: isn't it not technically correct to say there are four fundamental forces anymore?
answer: the higgs is not the mediator of a "fundamental" interaction. the "four forces" are gauge interactions, and are mediated by *vector* bosons (the higgs is a scalar). gauge theory isn't exactly a trivial subject so it's almost universally omitted in divulgation, but that's basically what is meant by fundamental interaction. the higgs' coupling to fermions instead is a simple, non gauged, yukawa coupling. about the x and y boson, these are hypothetical gauge bosons of most gut (grand unification theory) proposal. a gut is a single gauge interaction unifying the electroweak and strong interactions into a single gauge group, not an additional gauge interaction. finally, it's important to say that the subdivision of the gauge interactions, along with the subsequent "counting", it's somewhat arbitrary and at the very least a bit technical. the scheme is as such: - gravity is a gauge interaction but it's quite different from the others, so set it aside - the standard model is a gauge theory over the group u(1)×su(2)×su(3). this group is semisimple, not simple ("simple" is a tecnical term) and decomposes into three factors, which are - u(1), which is weak hypercharge, mediated by a boson usually called b - su(2), weak isospin, mediated by three bosons w^1 , w^2 , w^3 - su(3), the color or strong interaction, mediated by eight gluons. this makes four gauge interactions if the criterion is that the generators between two different interactions commute. now, as a consequence of the higgs mechanism, there is a certain mixing that happens in the u(1)×su(2) sector (electroweak). basically the b and w^3 bosons are mixed into the photon and the z^0 , while w^1 and w^2 are recombined into the w^+ and w^- . note that the total number of gauge bosons hasn't changed! so instead of weak isospin and hypercharge at low energy one usually talks about - the em gauge interaction, mediated by the photon and with gauge group u(1) (but it's a different copy of u(1) than weak hypercharge) - the "weak force", which by itself isn't a full gauge interaction and is really a weird hybrid thing reflecting its "mixed" origin, mediated by the ws and the z. that's the list that is usually given and it still gives four.

question: what does it mean when we say that the four fundamental forces are "unified" at high energies?
answer: it means that they are all described by a single field theory, in which a certain local symmetry (a gauge symmetry) is restored at a high enough interaction energy. above that energy, interactions behave a certain way which respects that symmetry. below that energy, the symmetry is spontaneously broken and the interactions now behave differently; they do not respect the (newly-broken) symmetry but may still respect other unbroken symmetries, allowing some aspects of the interaction to be well-described as a different interaction with a different symmetry. this is the case, for example, in electroweak theory, in which the su(2) x u(1) symmetry describing an electroweak interaction is spontaneously broken, leaving behind a part of the interaction which still respects a u(1) symmetry (electromagnetism), plus a part of the interaction which doesn't (the weak interaction). (edits for correctness.) experiment is the only way to *know* for sure. but there can be strong theoretical hints. in quantum field theory, interactions are characterized by a coupling constant related to the strength of the interaction. though calling it a constant is something of a misnomer, because the coupling constants "run" with the interaction energy level, becoming stronger (or weaker) as the energy increases. one of the hints pointing at a "grand unified theory" that unifies the strong and electroweak interactions is the observation that under certain assumptions, the coupling constants for each of these separate interactions approaches the same value at a much higher energy level -- the "gut scale" which is currently way, way beyond scales that we have the capacity to probe via experiment. because the unified symmetry is broken at low energies; it isn't respected anymore so the character of the forces change. they are describable by the same theory. the same theory just makes phenomenologically different predictions at lower energy levels when the symmetry is broken than it does at higher energy levels when the symmetry is not broken. hope that helps!
